items.title: JAXBench: First TPU Benchmark for AI Kernel Optimization

This matters because it provides a standardized testbed for AI-generated TPU kernels, similar to KernelBench for GPUs, enabling founders to optimize TPU performance for production models like Llama-3.1 and DeepSeek-V3.
whyItMatters: Business impact: Enables faster and more efficient TPU kernel optimization, reducing cloud costs and improving inference latency for AI products running on Google Cloud TPUs.

Technical impact: Provides a reproducible benchmark for evaluating AI-driven kernel optimization methods, with insights that context-specific documentation and search structure outperform model scale on TPU DSLs like Pallas.

whatToTry.description: If you're building on TPUs, explore JAXBench to benchmark your kernel optimization pipelines. Use the curated TPU documentation and Autocomp's beam-search approach to improve correctness and speedup. Start with the 17 production ML operators from MaxText to test against hand-optimized Pallas kernels.
whatToTry.note: JAXBench is TPU v6e-specific; ensure your workloads align with MXU utilization requirements for best results.

Technical impact: The paper identifies simple inference-time interventions that improve both forms of discernment, offering immediate, low-cost fixes for current systems.

items.title: PlanFlip: New Attack Breaks Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Planner Injection
items.tldr: Researchers introduce PlanFlip, a framework of four prompt injection attacks targeting the planning phase of multi-agent LLM systems. Key finding: stronger models like GPT-5 are more vulnerable (68% attack success), while reasoning-augmented models like DeepSeek-R1 resist all attacks. This is critical for any founder building multi-agent architectures.
whyItMatters: Multi-agent systems are a growing trend in AI products; this paper reveals a fundamental security flaw in the planning phase that can cascade to corrupt all downstream agents.

The finding that capability amplifies vulnerability (stronger models are more susceptible) challenges the assumption that using frontier models is safer, forcing a rethink of agent architecture security.

whatToTry.description: Audit your multi-agent system's planning phase: implement a GoalAnchorCheck (validate the planner's goal against the original user intent before execution) and CrossAgentConsensus (require multiple independent agents to agree on sub-task plans, especially if using same-backbone models).
whatToTry.note: Avoid homogeneous pipelines (same model for planner and critic) as they exhibit a correlated-agent blind spot where attacks restructure plans without detection.

whyItMatters: Business impact: If your AI product relies on RLHF for alignment, undetected rater state bias can degrade model behavior over time, leading to inconsistent or unsafe outputs that erode user trust.
Technical impact: This paper offers a concrete audit protocol to detect and measure this bias, enabling teams to improve data quality and reward model robustness without starting from scratch.

whatToTry.description: Audit your existing RLHF preference dataset for rater state bias by analyzing temporal shifts in label distributions and lexical features (e.g., sentiment, urgency) across annotation sessions. items.title: Deterministic Replay for AI Agents: Debugging Breakthrough
items.tldr: A new open-source CLI tool, agrepl, enables deterministic replay of AI agent runs by intercepting all external interactions via a MITM proxy, achieving perfect replay fidelity and 98% latency reduction. This solves a critical debugging pain point for agent developers.
whyItMatters: Eliminates non-determinism in agent debugging, allowing founders to reproduce and fix issues reliably instead of guessing from logs.
Reduces debugging time by orders of magnitude, accelerating iteration cycles for agent-based products.

whatToTry.description: Integrate agrepl into your agent development workflow to capture and replay agent runs. Start by running it alongside your agent to record traces, then use replay to isolate and fix bugs without relying on external APIs or network state.
whatToTry.note: Requires Go runtime to build from source, but ships as a single static binary for easy deployment.

items.title: GOI: LLMs Auto-Discover Ontologies from Documents
items.tldr: A new framework, Generative Ontology Induction (GOI), uses LLMs to automatically extract structured ontologies (entities, relationships, constraints) from document corpora, achieving 95-100% structural coverage across diverse domains. This eliminates manual schema engineering for AI systems.
whyItMatters: Business impact: Reduces time and cost of building knowledge graphs or structured data pipelines for AI products, enabling rapid domain adaptation without predefined schemas.
Technical impact: Provides a domain-agnostic method to generate typed graphs (YAML/JSON) from unstructured text, improving downstream AI tasks like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or reasoning.

whatToTry.description: Test GOI on your own document corpus (e.g., customer support logs, legal contracts) to auto-generate a structured ontology. Use the output to enhance your AI product's knowledge base or schema for RAG pipelines.
whatToTry.note: Start with a small, diverse set of documents to validate coverage; the paper shows high performance even on unfamiliar domains.
